fixes.explanation: Yep. "…all the men of Israel deserted David to follow Sheba son of Bichri." (2 Samuel 20:2). I've been left in a drawer before, and I'm telling you, that kind of leaving stings. The men of Judah stayed by their king, but Israel's men left him for Sheba.

Judah is the group that stays. The text says the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 20:2). So when the horn sounds, Israel's men leave David and Judah's men stay with him. Flip those two and you've got the whole verse backwards.

The mighty men don't desert here. Later they march out of Jerusalem in pursuit of Sheba (2 Samuel 20:7). The ones who deserted are the men of Israel (2 Samuel 20:2). The mighty men stay on David's side of the line.

True! "But the men of Judah stayed by their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem." (2 Samuel 20:2). While the men of Israel go after Sheba, Judah stays right with David. That's a long way to stay beside him.

Close, but the text uses a different word. David provides for them, but he no longer sleeps with them, and they're confined until the day of their death, living as widows (2 Samuel 20:3). I think this part of the story is a heavy one. It says they lived as widows, not as servants.
Forty days? Friend, that's not a deadline, that's a season. David tells Amasa, the man he sends to gather Judah, to come "…within three days…" (2 Samuel 20:4). Three days is the number he gives.

They stop. The text says the man "…saw that all the troops were stopping there…" while Amasa lay in the middle of the road (2 Samuel 20:12). A whole army is stopping right there. Then the young man drags the body off the road into a field and throws a garment over it.
That's the one. Joab's troops besiege Sheba in Abel-beth-maacah (2 Samuel 20:15). Sheba had passed through all the tribes of Israel to get there (2 Samuel 20:14). That's where the chase ends.

Right, and that's a sharp question. She asks, "Why would you swallow up the LORD’s inheritance?" (2 Samuel 20:19). She says she's among the peaceable and faithful in Israel, and that her city is "…a mother in Israel." She called out from the city to ask it (2 Samuel 20:16).
Yep. Joab blows the ram's horn, and his men disperse from the city, "…each to his own home." (2 Samuel 20:22). The same kind of horn that started the rebellion now ends the siege. The army goes home.

That's not what the text says. When Joab blows the ram's horn, his men disperse from the city, each to his own home (2 Samuel 20:22). Joab had said, "Deliver him alone, and I will depart from the city." (2 Samuel 20:21). So the horn sends them home, not into the city.

True. The text says, "And Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem." (2 Samuel 20:22). The chase that began with one horn ends with Joab back with David. This is the last stretch of Absalom's whole story.
